papers.title: PHOTONIC CRYSTAL MICROROBOTICS AT THE LIMIT FLAGSHIP 12/30 | STARLI INSTITUTE XXIV | GROUP B This prospective research monograph examines whether bandgap engineering and localized photonic crystal modes can enable physically predictable, reversible optical manipulation of microscopic agents when actual device geometry, absorption, hydrodynamic flow, surface adhesion, thermal limits, and task cost are fully considered. The three core couplings are photonic bands, microstructure response, and controllable motion. The book separates optical modes from attributable electromagnetic momentum transfer, and further separates externally steered particles or cells from autonomous microrobots. Its falsifiable research design compares two lattice-defect geometries, source-frequency interventions, local thermal controls, optimized free-space optical tweezers, non-periodic waveguide traps, and blinded second-chip replication. High Q or strong local field alone is not accepted as evidence of useful lower-power microrobotic performance. The manuscript contains 778 pages, approximately 119,409 English words in chapter openings and substantive chapter-body pages, 30 mathematical derivation signposts with mapped chapters and research questions, 82 research chapters, 410 individually paginated scientific study units, 200 detailed Research Gates, and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. An external DOI evidence ledger clarifies which physical contexts are supported by published work; four existing STARLI monographs supply intellectual genealogy, not experimental corroboration. An Excel research atlas offers equation-chapter-Gate-DOI navigation. A research Gate poses a future experiment, not a completed trial. Each door may be falsified, reinterpreted, or developed into a more testable hypothesis. The project prioritizes measurable physical mechanism, credible classical comparators, complete power and loss accounting, reproducible material controls, and release/recovery of agents. Negative outcomes are intentionally preserved as routes for later human and AI research successors.

papers.title: Autonomous Regenerative Cities and Public Life Maintenance Infrastructure at the Limit English Publication Description STARLI Flagship 24 30 Physicalized Models 82 Chapters 200 Research Gates Autonomous Regenerative Cities and Public Life Maintenance Infrastructure at the Limit is a high-density research monograph on whether cities can organize maintenance, rehabilitation, local biomanufacturing, monitoring, and minimum life-support services as reliable public infrastructure without creating unequal protection or irreversible dependence. The book separates installed capacity from delivered care, population sensing from individual diagnosis, automation from public obligation, and total throughput from equitable access. Consent, data minimization, manual alternatives, vendor substitution, and minimum service during shutdown remain hard boundaries rather than optional objectives. Thirty physicalized models connect capacitated service flows, queues, triage floors, network cuts, interdependent cascades, percolation, restoration scheduling, availability, surge capacity, swarm routing, spares, distributed microfactories, cold-chain viability, water-energy-health closure, islanded power, aggregate sensing, anomaly detection, differential privacy, federated robustness, consent automata, exit reachability, information minimization, social welfare, robust allocation, accessibility, interoperability, cyber-physical degradation, common-cause reliability, lifecycle burden, and joint public qualification. Eighty-two chapters each open with a governing gold equation and develop five one-page research sections. Two hundred Research Gates challenge the system with blackouts, communications partitions, hidden high-need populations, queue backlogs, privacy composition, consent withdrawal, inventory delay, vendor bankruptcy, and blind transfer to a second community. The work is a public-infrastructure research framework rather than an authorization for medical diagnosis or autonomous public deployment. Loss of minimum care, worsening group disparity, coerced participation, exhausted privacy budgets, unavailable manual fallback, failed exit, and successor lockout are noncompensable vetoes. Its Phoenix Answer Embryo, the Regenerative City Service Charter, binds public obligations, demand, capacity, outages, restoration, protected-group denominators, consent, retained data, refusal, exit, vendor interfaces, community testimony, independent audit, and successor control into one durable public evidence object. papers.title: FEDERATED SWARM LEARNING FOR PERSONALIZED BCI AT THE LIMIT STARLI RESEARCH WORKS | INSTITUTE XXIV | FLAGSHIP 23 Feng Cheng-en 33 × Starli PUBLICATION DESCRIPTION (COPY-READY) Can brain–computer interface systems learn from multiple laboratories and microrobotic sensing platforms without transferring raw neural recordings, reproducing device-specific shortcuts, or sacrificing the least-represented participants? This research monograph explores that question through the coupling of local swarm learning, privacy-preserving collaboration, and out-of-site generalization. The volume treats federation as a testable scientific and governance architecture—not an automatic privacy guarantee. It distinguishes confidential transport, secure aggregation, formal differential privacy, machine-unlearning claims, and genuine downstream withdrawal of model influence. It examines non-identically distributed neural data, sensor drift, personalized calibration, negative transfer, client-level poisoning, subgroup equity, and the difficult question of who may authorize a model update or a subsequent BCI-mediated action. Its research structure includes 30 linked mathematical derivation and definition plates; 82 chapters, each with five separately paginated research sections; 200 detailed Research Gates that offer future investigators falsifiable experimental entry points; and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos designed for revision, disconfirmation, and scientific handoff. A 20-record DOI evidence ledger anchors established methods while keeping proposed neurovascular microrobot integrations clearly distinct from demonstrated evidence. The central research challenge is not simply to improve average federated accuracy. It is to determine when shared structure remains predictive at previously unseen sites, when local autonomy is the scientifically stronger answer, and when the responsible choice is to abstain, revert, or retire a model. This is a non-clinical, hypothesis-generating research atlas, not evidence of validated human neurovascular microrobots, a clinically proven BCI, or guaranteed data privacy.

papers.summary: This archive supports a study of batch formation on material-extrusion 3D printers when each order has a due date. Parts are packed onto build platforms by four nesting engines (Guillotine, Skyline, and a pair of bottom-left-fill variants); the resulting batches are ordered on one to four identical machines so that total tardiness is as small as possible. The study compares three ways of choosing the destroy-and-repair moves of a local search: a random choice (iterated greedy), an adaptive choice based on the success history of each move (ALNS), and a policy trained by reinforcement learning.

papers.title: Autonomous Laboratories and Foundry Scientific Discovery at the Limit A machine does not discover a mechanism until it creates evidence that could defeat it Core coupling Autonomous experiment x active learning x scientific falsification Research scale 30 linked derivations x 82 chapters x 410 research sections x 200 detailed Research Gates Main result A falsifiable framework for generating, attacking and eliminating process mechanisms rather than confusing recipe optimization with scientific discovery. Series lineage Semiconductor Foundry Technologies x Intelligent Nanomanufacturing - Flagship 20 Publication Abstract This monograph asks whether an autonomous foundry laboratory can do more than optimize an existing recipe. It develops a research architecture in which the system must register competing process mechanisms, identify what its sensors can and cannot distinguish, choose experiments for model discrimination, preserve negative evidence, and issue counterfactual predictions that survive a new tool or fab. Yield improvement, simulation fit, and automation speed are treated as useful engineering outcomes but not as proof of a new mechanism. The central falsifiable proposition is that active experiments chosen to separate rival predictions should reduce the set of observationally equivalent mechanisms and improve preregistered counterfactual forecasts under the same sample, metrology, time, energy, and safety budget as expert DOE and strong safe Bayesian optimization. If the experiment cannot distinguish the models, if failures are selectively forgotten, if the acquisition function exploits a biased proxy, or if cross-tool predictions fail, the scientific claim is narrowed, split, or stopped. Scientific Position and Hard Boundary The work begins with bounded thin-film, deposition, etch, interface, and defect-mechanism challenges in simulation, digital-physical twins, test vehicles, and low-risk equipment states. Autonomous execution is permitted only through typed process intent, equipment capability contracts, explicit authorization, independent metrology, abort logic, and recoverable physical states. No information-gain score may override safety, material irreversibility, chain of custody, environmental obligations, worker protection, or equipment interlocks. Candidate Research Expression Dsci = Delta H of competing models + counterfactual information - sample cost - unsafe risk - hype penalty • Delta H measures reduction in uncertainty over the preregistered mechanism set. • Counterfactual information rewards predictions about interventions or new platforms that were not used for fitting. • Sample cost includes material, metrology, time, energy, and opportunity cost. • Unsafe risk is a hard feasibility concern, not a term that can be purchased by predicted knowledge. • The hype penalty prevents an engineering improvement from being narrated as a causal discovery. Five Layer Research Architecture 01 Competing Mechanism Contract Register rival mechanisms, observable signatures, claim levels, strong baselines, and hard boundaries. 02 Observability and Evidence Graph Map sensors, latent state, calibration ancestry, identifiability, and equivalent model sets. 03 Discriminating Active Experiment Choose controls, interventions, and fidelities for information under sample, energy, and risk budgets. 04 Refutation Memory and Safe Execution Compile typed experiments, preserve failures, detect misspecification, abort safely, and record why models were rejected. 05 Independent Transfer and Successor Choice Demand cross-tool counterfactual predictions, third-party replay, and the right to split, downgrade, or retire a mechanism. Minimum Verifiable Prototype Two process mechanisms are constructed to explain the same historical thin-film or etch observations. Expert DOE, safe Bayesian optimization, and the autonomous discovery policy receive matched samples, metrology, wall time, energy, and safety envelopes. Before the hidden outcomes are revealed, each freezes its hypotheses, predicted signatures, next experiment, acquisition value, uncertainty, and stopping rule. The decisive test is whether independent terminal metrology and a new intervention eliminate or sharply narrow one mechanism, not whether the system merely finds a better recipe. Research Contributions • Separates optimization, prediction, mechanism discrimination, causal support, and cross-platform scientific claims. • Connects observability, identifiability, Fisher information, Bayesian experimental design, causal intervention, and model criticism. • Treats negative results, failed experiments, calibration ancestry, manual corrections, and eliminated models as first-class scientific records. • Maps thirty distinct derivations to chapter, experiment, and Research Gate corridors. • Provides eighty-two chapters with five research pages per chapter: boundary, identifiability, minimum test, adversarial refutation, and successor route.
